deep.reconstruction:
This page is not a derivation. It is a hand-drawn finding chart titled 'Lauf der Pallas 1806 2 Febr – 13 März' (path of the minor planet Pallas, 2 Feb to 13 Mar 1806).

Coordinates (my reading):
- The bottom scale (78 at left down to 68 at right) is right ascension in degrees. It increases to the left, as on a sky chart.
- The right scale (11 at top to 24 at bottom) is declination in degrees. Checking the labelled stars against modern positions precessed back to about 1806 shows these are SOUTHERN declinations (−11° to −24°). The field is the constellation Lepus.

Star identifications (my checks):
- ε (large star at about α=74.3°, δ=−22.7°) is ε Leporis. Its J2000 position (α=76.365°, δ=−22.371°) precesses back 194 years to about 74.31°, −22.63°.
- The star labelled λ near the left edge (α≈77.55°, δ≈−13.35°) matches λ Lep, precessed to about 77.6°, −13.37°.
- The star labelled μ (α≈76.0°, δ≈−16.4°) matches μ Lep (precessed about 75.98°, −16.43°).
- The bright star on the track at about 76.0°, −13.2° matches κ Lep.
- The bright star at about 75.7°, −12.0° matches ι Lep.
- The scale reading and precession agree to within about 0.1°. So the stars were plotted carefully from a contemporary catalogue (Bode / Lalande / Piazzi era).

The track: Pallas's apparent path is a nearly straight line from lower right to upper left.
- It starts at 2 Feb, at about α≈69.2°, δ≈−24°.
- It ends at 13 Mar, at about α≈78°, δ≈−10.6°.
- Dated ticks are every 3 days: 2, 5, 8, 11 Feb, 14, 17, 20, 23, 26, 1 März, 4, 7, 10, 13. That is 14 points over 39 days. 1806 is not a leap year, so 26 Feb + 3 days = 1 Mar.
- The total arc is about 15–16° in 39 days, roughly 0.4°/day. This is direct motion toward the north-east, plausible for Pallas some weeks after opposition, given its high inclination.

Purpose: the positions were presumably taken from Gauss's own ephemeris of Pallas, computed from his orbital elements. The chart lets an observer recognise the planet among field stars.

Other features:
- A short secondary line segment or labels near (70.7°, −21°), read by the transcriber as '19' and '1?', may be star numbers or a correction to the track. They are uncertain.
- The faint concentric ovals in the background, including a ghost 'VESTA', are show-through of the orbit diagram on folio 219 (Pallas, Juno, Vesta, Ceres, Erde). They are not part of this chart.
- The next page continues the observing context ('Neu bestimmte Sterne febr. 13', positions near α 69–71°, δ 20°). This is consistent with Gauss checking comparison stars near the planet on 13 Feb.
errors: No mathematical errors. The date sequence is internally consistent (3-day steps, Feb 1806 having 28 days), and the identified Lepus stars lie at the correct precessed positions to within about 0.1°.
The chart does not mark declinations as south; the sign is implicit.

results.what: Hand-plotted finding chart of the apparent path of Pallas, 2 Feb – 13 Mar 1806, at 3-day intervals among the stars of Lepus
results.modern_name: Ephemeris finding chart (apparent geocentric path of a minor planet)
results.usually_credited_to: Standard practice of contemporary astronomers (Gauss, Olbers, von Zach's Monatliche Correspondenz)

deep.surprise_reason: Gauss computing ephemerides of Pallas in 1805–06 and supporting observations is well documented. A finding chart is routine working material with no new mathematics.

checkable.asserts: Feb 2 to Mar 13 1806 spans 39 days = 13 intervals of 3 days (14 plotted points)
Precessed RA of eps Lep for about 1806 is approximately 74.3 deg, matching the chart's epsilon at bottom-scale ~74.3
Precessed Dec of eps Lep for about 1806 is approximately -22.63 deg, matching the chart (~22.7 on the right scale, south)
Precessed RA of mu Lep is approximately 75.98 deg, matching the star labelled mu at ~76.0
Mean apparent motion of Pallas over the plotted interval is about 0.4 deg/day

transcription_corrections: The right-margin scale is declination, south (−11° to −24°); the bottom scale is right ascension in degrees (78 to 68). The field is Lepus.
Track labels from bottom to top are 2, 5, 8, 11 Februar, 14, 17, 20, 23, 26, 1 März, 4, 7, 10, 13. The lowest '2[?]' is indeed 2 (Feb 2), and an unlabelled '5' tick lies between 2 and 8.
'19[?]' and '1[?]' near α≈70.7°, δ≈−21° are not track dates. They are probably star numbers or a correction mark.
Star label 'κ[?]' at the top (α≈75.7°, δ≈−12.0°) is more likely ι Lep. The bright star on the track at α≈76.0°, δ≈−13.2° is κ Lep. 'ι[?]' at α≈76.0°, δ≈−16.4° is μ Lep.
'ζ[?]' at α≈78°, δ≈−19° cannot be ζ Lep (RA ≈ 85° in 1806). The label is uncertain.
The faint circles and the ghost word 'VESTA' are show-through from the orbit diagram on f. 219, not content of this page.
